elements.quote: No evidence-based treatment for COVID-19 currently exist to augment widely used supportive care protocols [7]. To control the growing COVID-19 pandemic, we rely on quarantine, isolation, and infection-control measures to prevent disease spread [7] and on supportive care, including oxygen and mechanical ventilation, for infected patients. Many randomized clinical trials assessing the effects of different potential treatments for COVID-19 are currently underway.
elements.reason: The text describes the current state of knowledge (no evidence-based treatments exist, trials are underway) and the uncertainty regarding effective treatments.

elements.quote: However, a single trial can rarely validly assess the effects of any intervention, and there is an urgent need to continuously surveil and update the aggregated evidence base so that effective interventions, if such exist, are implemented in clinical practice [8].
elements.reason: The text explains the importance and need for the review, specifically the need to aggregate evidence from multiple trials to inform clinical practice.

elements.quote: Wehave identified 4 important reviews that are comparable to our present project [77-80]. The first is a network meta-analysis just published in BMJ [77]. However, at the time of publication, this project did not include all relevant trials... The second project is a literature review published in JAMA... Moreover, this review was only a narrative review without meta-analytic methods and trial sequential analysis [78].
elements.reason: The authors identify similar reviews and explain the need for their own review by highlighting limitations in the existing ones (e.g., missing trials, lack of meta-analytic methods).

This is a broad systematic review covering all possible interventions for COVID-19, rather than a review of a specific intervention or class of interventions where a mechanism of action would be relevant or feasible to describe.
The review does not focus on a single complex intervention or delivery context that would require a logic model.

elements.quote: There is a need for a living systematic review evaluating the beneficial and harmful effects of all possible interventions for treatment of COVID-19.
elements.reason: The objective of the review is explicitly stated in the Author Summary, identifying the goal to evaluate beneficial and harmful effects of all possible interventions for COVID-19 treatment.

elements.quote: Primary outcomes were all-cause mortality and serious adverse events... Secondary outcomes were admission to intensive care... receipt of mechanical ventilation... receipt of renal replacement therapy... quality of life, and nonserious adverse events.
elements.reason: The review defines the scope of the intervention effects (treatments for COVID-19) and explicitly lists the primary and secondary outcomes, which constitutes the PICO framework (Population: COVID-19 patients, Intervention: treatments, Comparison: implied standard care/placebo, Outcomes: listed).

elements.quote: This is the first edition of a living systematic review of randomized clinical trials comparing the effects of all treatment interventions for participants in all age groups with COVID-19.
elements.reason: The review specifies the study design (randomized clinical trials), the population (participants in all age groups with COVID-19), and the intervention (all treatment interventions) used to determine eligibility.

elements.quote: Trials were included irrespective of language, publication status, publication year, and publication type.
elements.reason: The review explicitly states the eligibility criteria regarding report characteristics, including language, publication status, and publication year.
The manuscript does not explicitly distinguish between excluding studies because outcomes were not measured versus excluding them because results were not reported.

elements.quote: Weplanned to conduct aggregate data meta-analyses, trial sequential analyses, network meta-analysis, and individual patient data meta-analyses.
elements.reason: The review specifies the types of syntheses planned and links them to the objective of comparing treatment interventions, with specific comparisons (e.g., dexamethasone vs standard care) detailed in the results.
While the review restricts inclusion to randomized clinical trials, no explicit rationale is provided for this restriction.

elements.quote: We searched all databases from their inception and until August 7, 2020.
elements.reason: The authors explicitly state the date the databases were last searched (August 7, 2020).

elements.quote: An information specialist searched the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL) in The Cochrane Library, Medical Literature Analysis and Retrieval System Online (MEDLINE Ovid), Excerpta Medica database (Embase Ovid), Latin American and Caribbean Health Sciences Literature (LILACS; Bireme), Science Citation Index Expanded (SCI-EXPANDED; Web of Science), Conference Proceedings Citation Index-Science (CPCI-S; Web of Science), BIOSIS (Web of Science), CINAHL (EBSCO host), Chinese Biomedical Literature Database (CBM), China Network Knowledge Information (CNKI), Chinese Science Journal Database (VIP), and Wafang Database to identify relevant trials.
elements.reason: The authors list the names of the bibliographic databases and their platforms/interfaces (e.g., MEDLINE Ovid, Embase Ovid, CINAHL EBSCO host). However, they do not report the available coverage dates for these databases, only stating they searched from inception.

elements.quote: To identify unpublished trials, we searched clinical trial registries (e.g., clinicaltrials.gov, clinicaltrialregister.eu, who.int/ictrp, chictr.org.cn) of Europe, USA, and China
elements.reason: The authors name the clinical trial registries searched. No specific date restrictions are mentioned, implying no restrictions were applied.

elements.quote: Primary outcomes were all-cause mortality and serious adverse events (as defined by the International Conference on Harmonation-Good Clinical Practice [ICH-GCP] guidelines) [9,16]. Secondary outcomes were admission to intensive care (as defined by trialists), receipt of mechanical ventilation (as defined by trialists), receipt of renal replacement therapy (as defined by trialists), quality of life, and nonserious adverse events. We classified nonserious adverse events as any adverse event not assessed as serious according to the ICH-GCP definition. Wechose to add time to clinical improvement as a post hoc outcome.
elements.reason: The manuscript lists and defines the primary and secondary outcomes, including definitions for serious and nonserious adverse events and references to trialist definitions for others.

elements.quote: For all outcomes, we used the trial results reported at maximum follow-up.
elements.reason: The authors specify a general rule for time frame ('maximum follow-up') for all outcomes, but do not specify the time frame for each individual outcome domain (e.g., mortality at 28 days vs 60 days), though they do mention specific time points in the results sections (e.g., text_30 mentions 15 and 28 days).
The manuscript does not explicitly state whether all results compatible with each outcome domain (e.g., all measures, time points, analyses) were sought.

Since the manuscript does not state whether all compatible results were sought, this conditional element cannot be evaluated, but there is no evidence provided that they restricted the search for compatible results.

elements.reason: The authors explicitly state the effect measures used for dichotomous outcomes (risk ratios) and planned measures for continuous outcomes (mean differences and standardized mean differences).

The manuscript does not describe the specific process used to decide which studies were eligible for each synthesis (e.g., how studies were grouped by intervention or outcome). While the authors reference the Cochrane Handbook and their protocol, and list the comparisons performed in the results, they do not explicitly describe the process of mapping studies to these synthesis groups.

elements.quote: We conducted both randomeffects (Inverse Variance, DerSimonian-Laird) and fixed-effect (Mantel-Haenszel) meta-analyses for all analyses and chose the most conservative result as our primary result [12,18,21,22]. Weused trial sequential analysis to control for random errors [23-31]. Trial sequential analysis estimates the diversity-adjusted required information size (DARIS), which is the number of participants needed in a meta-analysis to detect or reject a certain intervention effect. Statistical heterogeneity was quantified by calculating inconsistency (I square) for traditional meta-analyses and diversity (D square) for trial sequential analysis. We used GRADE to assess the certainty of evidence. We downgraded imprecision in GRADE by 2 levels if the accrued number of participants were below 50% of the DARIS and one level if between 50% and 100% of DARIS.
elements.reason: The manuscript describes the statistical methods used for synthesis, including the choice of meta-analysis models (fixed and random effects), the use of trial sequential analysis to control for random errors, and the specific methods for assessing heterogeneity and certainty of evidence (GRADE), which constitute the methods for data synthesis.

While the manuscript lists numerous 'Summary of findings' tables in the Supporting Information (chunk_id: text_36), it does not describe the methods used to construct these tables or the specific data included in them.

elements.quote: Random-effects meta-analysis showed no evidence of a difference between remdesivir versus placebo on all-cause mortality... ( Fig 2; S5 Table ). Visual inspection of the forest plot and measures to quantify heterogeneity (I 2 = 58%) indicated heterogeneity... The manuscript does not describe the basis for ordering or grouping studies within the tables or graphs.
The manuscript uses standard graphical methods for systematic reviews (forest plots and trial sequential analysis plots), so there are no non-standard graphs requiring a rationale.

elements.quote: Our living systematic review also has limitations. The primary limitation is the paucity of trials currently available, and the results from the current meta-analyses are of low or very low certainty. This must be considered when interpreting our meta-analysis results. Secondly, the trials that we succeeded in including were all at risks of systematic errors and random errors. Third, it was not possible to perform the planned individual patient data meta-analyses, network-meta-analysis, or the planned subgroup analyses because of the lack of relevant data. ... Fourth, we included 'time to clinical improvement' as an outcome post hoc. ... Fifth, all trials differed in the included participants' disease severity at trial intake ... Sixth, the included trials assessed the outcomes at different time points ... Seventh, some data are included from preprints, and these might be subject to change following peer review.
